title: Singin' Hinnies
subtitle: Northumbrian griddle cakes with currants and lard
excerpt: Northumbrian currant cakes cooked on a dry griddle or iron pan, soft inside with a buttery, slightly crisp surface. Named for the sound they make as the fat sizzles on the hot iron.
sourceNotes: Dorothy Hartley, Food in England (1954), singin' hinnies documented as a traditional Northumbrian griddle cake. The name 'hinny' is a Northumbrian and Geordie term of endearment; 'singing' refers to the sizzling of the fat on the iron. Florence White, Good Things in England (1932), singin' hinnies as a regional speciality of Tyneside.

content.text: Singin' hinnies are Northumbrian currant griddle cakes: a rich, lard-enriched dough cooked on an ungreased iron pan until the outside is lightly crunchy and the inside is soft and slightly layered. They are very similar to Welsh cakes but larger and slightly richer. The name comes from the sizzling sound they make on the hot griddle, and from 'hinny', a local term of endearment used across Tyneside.

items.prepNote: cold, cubed (or replace with all butter)

content.text: Put {{self-raising-flour}} of flour in a bowl. Rub in {{salted-butter}} of cold butter and {{lard}} of cold lard until the mixture looks like coarse breadcrumbs.
Stir in {{caster-sugar}} of caster sugar and {{currants}} of currants. Add {{whole-milk}} of milk gradually, mixing until the dough just comes together. It should be firm and dry, not sticky.
On a floured surface, roll out to about 1 cm thick and cut into rounds with a 10 cm cutter. Gather the scraps and re-roll.
Heat a heavy, dry frying pan over medium-low heat without any fat. Cook the hinnies for 4 to 5 minutes per side until golden and cooked through. They should sizzle gently when they hit the pan.
Split open and serve warm with butter.

rows.symptom: Dark on the outside, raw in the middle
rows.fix: Keep the pan at medium-low throughout. These are thick cakes and need a long, steady heat to cook through.

rows.cause: Currants on the surface of the dough exposed to high heat
rows.fix: Press any surface currants back into the dough before cooking. Lower the heat if they start burning.

rows.symptom: Dough is too soft and sticky to roll
rows.fix: Add milk a little at a time and stop as soon as the dough comes together. Refrigerate for 10 minutes to firm up.

rows.symptom: Hinnies have no sizzle or browning
rows.cause: Pan not preheated or fat content too low
rows.fix: Make sure the pan is properly hot before the cakes go on. The sizzle comes from the lard in the dough meeting the hot iron.

content.text: Singin hinnies come from Northumbria, particularly Tyneside. They are the northern English equivalent of the Welsh cake: a griddle cake made from similar ingredients but with a slightly higher fat content. Dorothy Hartley documented them as part of a pattern of British regional griddle breads. They developed where coal-fired iron ranges replaced open-hearth baking.
